Products, services and ideas flow from the organization to the market
questions.explanation: The marketing process is 'a process that focuses on consumer needs': it begins by identifying needs, not by building a product first (that is production-era thinking). The other three statements describe Figure 1-2 accurately.

questions.stem: Why does the chapter describe the marketing process as 'a process that focuses on consumer needs'?
options: It ends with consumer needs only after the firm has maximized its production output
It replaces profit with consumer needs as the organization's one and only goal
It treats consumer needs as an uncontrollable environmental force to be monitored
It begins by discovering needs, then designs the mix to satisfy them before profits follow
questions.explanation: Needs drive the whole sequence: they are identified first, the marketing mix is managed to satisfy them, and profits (or objectives) result. The process does not drop profit - realizing profits is its third step.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'The marketing process and the marketing concept are the same thing.' Which correction is best?
options: The process applies only to non-profit groups; the concept applies only to for-profit firms
The process is three steps: needs, mix, profits; the concept is satisfying needs while meeting goals
The process is a philosophy about serving customers; the concept is a three-step sequence of actions
The process is the 4 Ps of the mix; the concept is the five uncontrollable environmental forces
questions.explanation: The marketing process is a sequence of steps; the marketing concept is the guiding idea behind it. The second option simply swaps the two definitions, and both apply to for-profit and non-profit organizations.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly shows the evolution of business philosophies?
options: Production → marketing → sales → relationship/societal
Marketing → production → sales → relationship/societal
Production → sales → marketing → relationship/societal
Sales → production → marketing → relationship/societal
questions.explanation: Firms first focused on efficient production (demand exceeded supply), then on selling their output as competition grew, then on consumer needs (marketing orientation), and today on long-term relationships and society's well-being.

questions.stem: In 1912, a Montreal stove manufacturer could sell every stove it built because demand far exceeded supply, so its managers focused on making stoves as efficiently as possible. Which orientation did the firm have?
options: Societal marketing orientation
Marketing orientation
Sales orientation
Production orientation
questions.explanation: A production orientation focuses on producing goods efficiently and fits the early-1900s condition of demand exceeding supply. A sales orientation emerged later, once competition grew and firms had to push their output.

questions.stem: Facing new competitors and warehouses full of unsold vacuum cleaners, Hartwell Appliances hires a large door-to-door sales force and pays big commissions to push its existing models. Which orientation does this reflect?
options: Relationship marketing orientation
Sales orientation
Production orientation
Marketing orientation
questions.explanation: Pushing products the firm has already made through aggressive selling and promotion is the sales orientation. A marketing orientation would start by finding out what customers need before deciding what to make.

questions.stem: What most clearly separates the marketing orientation from the sales orientation?
options: Marketing emerged when demand exceeded supply; sales emerged once competition grew
Marketing stresses long-term relationships and society; sales stresses consumer needs
Marketing begins with consumer needs; sales begins with the products the firm has already made
Marketing relies on promotion; sales relies mainly on efficient production
questions.explanation: The key difference is the starting point: the marketing orientation starts by discovering consumer needs, while the sales orientation pushes output the firm has already produced. 'Demand exceeded supply' describes the production era, and long-term relationships plus society describe today's relationship/societal orientation.

questions.stem: According to the evolution of business philosophies, why did many firms shift from a production orientation to a sales orientation?
options: Competition grew, so firms had to push their output to sell it
Consumers began demanding socially responsible business practices
Firms started sharing customer and competitor data across departments
Governments began banning efficient mass-production methods
questions.explanation: The production era worked because demand exceeded supply; as competition grew, firms needed selling and promotion to move what they produced. Demand for social responsibility belongs to today's societal era, and sharing data across departments describes a market orientation.

questions.stem: Ridgeline Credit Union in Calgary now measures success by how many members stay for ten years or more, and it publicly reports on its community investments and environmentally responsible lending. Which stage in the evolution of business philosophies does this reflect?
options: Production orientation
Sales orientation
Relationship/societal orientation
Marketing orientation
questions.explanation: Long-term relationships (members staying a decade) plus attention to society's well-being (community investment, responsible lending) mark today's relationship/societal orientation. The plain marketing orientation focuses on satisfying consumer needs without that added long-term relationship and societal emphasis.

questions.stem: The idea that an organization should strive to satisfy the needs of consumers while also trying to achieve the organization's goals is the:
options: marketing concept
sales orientation
societal marketing concept
market orientation
questions.explanation: This two-part idea (satisfy consumers + achieve organizational goals) is the marketing concept. The societal marketing concept adds a third element, society's well-being, and market orientation is the practical implementation of the marketing concept.

questions.stem: At Boreal Bikes in Thunder Bay, managers launch only models that customer research shows riders want, and only if the model can also meet the company's 25% margin target. Which idea guides Boreal?
options: Macromarketing
The marketing concept
Customer experience management
The production orientation
questions.explanation: Boreal balances both halves of the marketing concept: satisfying consumer needs (research-based models) and achieving organizational goals (the margin target). A production orientation would focus on making bikes efficiently regardless of what riders want.

questions.stem: How does the societal marketing concept differ from the marketing concept?
options: It focuses on pushing the firm's existing output through aggressive promotion
It drops the goal of satisfying consumer needs in favour of serving society
It requires collecting competitor information and sharing it across departments
It adds that needs be satisfied in a way that also provides for society's well-being
questions.explanation: The societal marketing concept keeps the marketing concept's goal of satisfying consumers but adds society's well-being. It does not abandon consumers; aggressive selling is the sales orientation, and sharing information across departments is market orientation.

questions.stem: A company claims to follow the marketing concept. Which practice is NOT consistent with that claim?
options: Making whatever is cheapest to produce, then pushing it with heavy discounts
Rejecting a popular product idea that could never meet its profit goals
Researching customer needs before developing any new products
Updating its offering whenever customer needs change over time
questions.explanation: Making whatever is cheapest and then pushing it ignores consumer needs (production and sales thinking). Rejecting an idea that cannot meet profit goals IS consistent with the marketing concept, because the concept includes achieving the organization's goals, not satisfying customers at any cost.

questions.stem: Firms that put great effort into implementing the marketing concept are said to have a market orientation.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Market orientation is the marketing concept put into practice: continuously collecting information about customers' needs and competitors' capabilities, sharing it across departments, and using it to create customer value.

questions.stem: An organization that focuses its efforts on continuously collecting information about customers' needs and competitors' capabilities, sharing this information across departments, and using the information to create customer values is said to:
options: stress the societal marketing concept
have a focus on macromarketing
have a nonprofit orientation
have a market orientation
be utilizing consumerism
questions.explanation: Collecting customer and competitor information, sharing it across departments and using it to create customer value is the definition of market orientation, the result of implementing the marketing concept. The societal marketing concept would add society's well-being, and macromarketing concerns a nation's aggregate flow of goods.

questions.stem: Every Monday, Tidewater Grocers' analytics team compiles loyalty-card data on shoppers' changing needs and a report on competitors' new services, sends both to the buying, store-operations and finance teams, and each team uses them to improve what customers get. Tidewater displays:
options: macromarketing
the societal marketing concept
a sales orientation
a market orientation
questions.explanation: All three components of market orientation are present: continuous collection of customer and competitor information, sharing across departments, and use of the information to create customer value. Nothing in the stem mentions society's well-being.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a component of a market orientation?
options: Collecting information about competitors' capabilities
Keeping customer information inside the marketing department
Continuously collecting information about customers' needs
Using the gathered information to create customer value
questions.explanation: A market orientation requires SHARING information across departments, not keeping it within marketing. Collecting customer and competitor information and using it to create value are the other components.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes market orientation from the marketing concept?
options: Market orientation is the underlying idea; the marketing concept is how a firm puts it into practice
Market orientation is a production-era philosophy; the marketing concept is the philosophy used today
Market orientation is the practical implementation (collect, share, use information); the marketing concept is the idea
Market orientation focuses on society's well-being; the marketing concept largely ignores customers
questions.explanation: The marketing concept is the idea (satisfy consumer needs while achieving organizational goals); firms that work hard at implementing it achieve a market orientation by collecting, sharing and using information. The second option reverses them.

questions.stem: Cedar & Pine Furniture's marketing team surveys customers, but the design and production teams never see the results, and nobody tracks what competitors offer. What should the firm do to become market oriented?
options: Sponsor a community program to adopt the societal marketing concept
Add competitor research and share all findings across departments so each can create customer value
Switch to a sales orientation to move existing inventory faster
Have the marketing team run customer surveys more often and keep the results in marketing
questions.explanation: Market orientation has three parts: continuously collect information on customers' needs AND competitors' capabilities, share it across departments, and use it to create customer value. Cedar & Pine already collects customer data, so more surveys kept inside marketing miss both gaps: competitor information and cross-department sharing.

questions.stem: The idea that organizations are part of a larger society and are accountable to that society for their actions is called:
options: customer relationship management
the marketing concept
corporate social responsibility
macromarketing
questions.explanation: That is the definition of corporate social responsibility (CSR). Macromarketing is also society-level, but it describes the aggregate flow of a nation's goods and services, not an organization's accountability for its actions.

questions.stem: Every summer, Prairie Sky Insurance designs and runs a free swimming-lessons program for children in Regina's inner-city neighbourhoods. Which type of CSR initiative is this?
options: Sponsorship and/or spearheading of community programs
Sponsorship of or involvement in fundraising for charitable organizations
A business philosophy that implements socially responsible practices
Customer relationship management aimed at policyholders
questions.explanation: Prairie Sky is spearheading a community program, the first CSR type on the slide. No charity is raising money (type 2), and the firm's overall business practices are not changing (type 3).

questions.stem: During April, Harbourfront Hardware in Halifax asks shoppers to donate at checkout to the Canadian Cancer Society and matches every dollar raised. Which type of CSR initiative is this?
options: Sponsorship and/or spearheading of community programs
Experiential marketing at the point of sale
A business philosophy that implements socially responsible practices
Sponsorship of or involvement in fundraising for charitable organizations
questions.explanation: Raising and matching money for a charity is the second CSR type: fundraising initiatives for charitable organizations. It is not the firm running its own community program (type 1) or changing how the entire business operates (type 3).

questions.stem: Polaris Apparel overhauls how it operates: it pays all suppliers a living wage, switches every product line to recycled fabric, and ties executive bonuses to emissions cuts. Which type of CSR initiative is this?
options: Partnership marketing with sustainable brands
A business philosophy that implements socially responsible practices
Sponsorship of or involvement in fundraising for charitable organizations
Sponsorship and/or spearheading of community programs
questions.explanation: When social responsibility is built into the way the whole business runs (sourcing, materials, pay incentives), it is the third CSR type: a business philosophy that implements socially responsible practices. No specific community program or charity fundraiser is involved.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the three types of CSR initiatives listed in the chapter?
options: Sponsoring or spearheading community programs
Sponsoring or taking part in fundraising for charities
Running a points program that rewards repeat customers
Adopting a business philosophy of socially responsible practices
questions.explanation: The three CSR types are community programs, charitable fundraising, and a socially responsible business philosophy. A points program rewarding repeat customers is a customer relationship (loyalty) tactic, not a CSR initiative.

questions.stem: Glenbow Beverages wants to move from the marketing concept to the societal marketing concept. Which change would best accomplish this?
options: Cutting sugar and using recyclable bottles while still meeting tastes and profit goals
Sharing competitor data across all departments every week to create customer value
Speeding up production lines to lower the cost of making each bottle
Hiring more salespeople to push existing inventory into more stores
questions.explanation: The societal marketing concept satisfies consumer needs (and organizational goals) in a way that also provides for society's well-being, which healthier drinks and recyclable packaging do. Faster production is production thinking, pushing inventory is sales thinking, and sharing competitor data is market orientation.

questions.stem: Nordic Outfitters' CEO says: 'We design only what customers say they need, priced so we still hit our profit target, but we will not use a cheaper fabric that pollutes local rivers, even though customers would never notice.' The final part of her statement goes beyond the marketing concept to reflect the:
options: market orientation
sales orientation
customer relationship management
societal marketing concept
questions.explanation: Satisfying customers while meeting profit goals is the marketing concept; refusing a cheaper input to protect society's well-being, even when customers would not notice, adds the societal dimension. Market orientation is about collecting, sharing and using customer and competitor information, which the statement does not describe.

questions.stem: Rajan's Wealth Software and Yi Capital Group, two top vendors of financial management software, have recently launched their own online trading exchange aimed at increasing the ease with which their customers can finance their new products and ideas. Both of these organizations provide exceptional, ongoing service to their business customers. These two organizations hope to benefit from:
options: customer relationship management
societal marketing concept
customer orientation
product valuation
none of the above
questions.explanation: CRM is the process of building and developing long-term relationships with customers by delivering customer value and satisfaction, and exceptional, ongoing service to business customers aims at exactly that. The societal marketing concept would require a focus on society's well-being, which the stem never mentions.

questions.stem: The process of building and developing long-term relationships with customers by delivering customer value and satisfaction is called:
options: the marketing concept
market orientation
customer experience management
customer relationship management
questions.explanation: This is the definition of CRM. Customer experience management concerns the customer's internal response to all aspects of the organization; the cue words here are 'long-term relationships' delivered through 'value and satisfaction'.

questions.stem: Linking an organization to its individual customers, employees, suppliers and other partners for their mutual long-term benefit is the definition of:
options: customer relationship management
relationship marketing
partnership marketing
macromarketing
questions.explanation: Relationship marketing links the organization not only to customers but also to employees, suppliers and other partners. CRM focuses on long-term relationships with customers specifically, so the mention of employees and suppliers is the cue. Partnership marketing is a formal association between brands.

questions.stem: Northwind Auto in Edmonton records each customer's service history, sends personalized maintenance reminders, and gives free winter-tire swaps to clients who have stayed five years or more. Northwind is practising:
options: customer relationship management
macromarketing
the production orientation
experiential marketing
questions.explanation: Tracking individual customers and rewarding long-time clients builds long-term relationships by delivering value and satisfaction, which is CRM. Experiential marketing would involve creating hands-on brand experiences, not ongoing relationship building.

questions.stem: Why do firms invest in customer relationship management rather than focusing only on individual sales?
options: To replace the 4 Ps of the marketing mix with a single, cheaper promotional tool
To control environmental forces such as the state of the economy and competitors
To keep customers returning long-term by delivering value and satisfaction
To lower production costs by making manufacturing more efficient and automated
questions.explanation: CRM's purpose is long-term relationships built on delivering customer value and satisfaction, so customers keep coming back. Environmental forces cannot be controlled by any marketing tool, and CRM works alongside the marketing mix rather than replacing it.

questions.stem: Which practice is NOT consistent with customer relationship management?
options: Tracking each customer's preferences to personalize future offers
Using high-pressure tactics to maximize one-time sales, ignoring repeat business
Providing exceptional ongoing service to existing business clients
Rewarding long-time customers with loyalty perks and early access
questions.explanation: CRM is about long-term relationships, so one-off, high-pressure selling that ignores repeat business contradicts it. Ongoing service, personalization and loyalty rewards all build long-term relationships through value and satisfaction.

questions.stem: Managing the internal response that customers have to all aspects of an organization and its offering is called:
options: customer experience management
customer value
experiential marketing
customer relationship management
questions.explanation: This is customer experience management; its cue words are 'internal response' and 'all aspects of an organization'. Experiential marketing is a promotional practice that creates hands-on brand experiences, and CRM is about long-term relationships built on value and satisfaction.

questions.stem: Aurora Hotels hires a team to map every guest touchpoint - the booking app, check-in, room scent, staff greetings and checkout emails - and redesigns any point where guests say they felt frustrated or ignored. Which practice is this?
options: Experiential marketing
Macromarketing
Customer experience management
Partnership marketing
questions.explanation: Managing guests' internal response across all aspects of the organization is customer experience management. Experiential marketing, the tempting look-alike, means creating hands-on brand events for consumers, not redesigning every service touchpoint.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes customer experience management from customer relationship management (CRM)?
options: Experience management applies only to organizational buyers; CRM applies only to ultimate consumers buying for households
Experience management is a production-era practice; CRM is a sales-era practice used to push inventory
Experience management builds long-term relationships through delivering value; CRM manages customers' feelings at each touchpoint
Experience management targets customers' internal response to every aspect of the firm; CRM targets long-term relationships via value and satisfaction
questions.explanation: The definitions differ in focus: customer experience management targets the customer's internal response to all aspects of the organization, while CRM targets long-term relationships through value and satisfaction. The second option swaps the definitions; in practice the two support each other.

questions.stem: Which statement about customer experience management is NOT correct?
options: It covers all aspects of the organization and its offering
It focuses only on the product itself, ignoring websites, staff and service
A positive experience can support long-term customer relationships
It concerns customers' internal response to the organization
questions.explanation: Customer experience management covers ALL aspects of the organization and its offering - the website, staff, service and the product - so 'only the product' is wrong. A good experience supports the long-term relationships CRM aims for.

questions.stem: A student confuses customer experience management with experiential marketing. Which example is experiential marketing rather than customer experience management?
options: An airline studies how travellers feel at each step from booking to baggage claim
A hotel retrains staff and updates its website so guests feel welcome at every touchpoint
A chip brand sets up a pop-up 'flavour lab' at a Toronto festival where visitors create and taste their own seasonings
A bank redesigns its app, branch greetings and follow-up calls after customers report feeling ignored
questions.explanation: Experiential marketing creates opportunities for consumers to interact directly with a brand, such as a hands-on festival pop-up. The other three options manage customers' internal response across the organization's touchpoints, which is customer experience management.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of an organizational buyer?
options: A mother buying milk for her young son
A computer programmer buying the latest game for his PlayStation
A store owner buying hand-painted slate signs to sell in her store
A botanist buying a rose bush for his home garden
A baseball player buying a t-ball set for his daughter
questions.explanation: Organizational buyers are manufacturers, wholesalers, retailers and government agencies that buy for their own use or for resale. The store owner is buying signs to resell; every other buyer is purchasing for personal or household use, which makes them ultimate consumers regardless of their occupation.

questions.stem: Priya, a dentist in Lethbridge, buys a laptop. In which situation is she acting as an organizational buyer?
options: She buys it for her clinic's front desk
She buys it as a birthday gift for her sister
She buys it to stream movies in her living room
She buys it for her teenage son's homework
questions.explanation: What matters is the purpose of the purchase. Buying for the clinic's own use makes Priya an organizational buyer; the other purchases are for personal or household use, so she would be an ultimate consumer even though she is a professional.

questions.stem: The same 24-pack of bottled water is bought by a Calgary family for a camping trip and by a convenience-store owner to sell from her cooler. What determines which buyer is the ultimate consumer?
options: The size of the order: small versus bulk quantities
The price paid: full retail versus a discounted price
The type of product: consumer goods versus industrial goods
The purpose of the purchase: household use versus resale
questions.explanation: Ultimate consumers buy for household use; organizational buyers buy for their own organizational use or for resale. The product here is identical, so the only thing that separates the two buyers is the purpose of the purchase.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an organizational buyer?
options: A dentist buying a gaming console for his den
A Canadian Tire dealer buying barbecues to resell
Alberta Health Services buying hospital beds
A Regina bakery buying flour to make bread
questions.explanation: The dentist is buying for household use, so he is an ultimate consumer despite his professional job - the classic job-title trap. A government agency buying for its own use, a manufacturer (bakery) buying inputs, and a retailer buying for resale are all organizational buyers.

questions.stem: A provincial ministry buys 500 snow shovels to sell at cost to seniors through community centres. How should the ministry be classified, and why?
options: Not a buyer at all, because no profit is made on the resale
Ultimate consumer, because the shovels will end up being used in seniors' households
Ultimate consumer, because government agencies are not businesses
Organizational buyer, because a government agency is buying for resale rather than household use
questions.explanation: Organizational buyers include government agencies that buy for their own use or for resale. The ministry is reselling (even at cost), so it is an organizational buyer; the seniors who later buy the shovels for home use are the ultimate consumers.

questions.stem: The benefits or customer value received by users of a product is called:
options: exchange
a value proposition
utility
customer satisfaction
questions.explanation: Utility is the benefit or customer value users receive from a product, and it comes in four types: form, place, time and possession. A value proposition is a promised set of benefits, not the benefit actually received through use.

questions.stem: Sunrise Coffee opens a kiosk beyond security in the Edmonton International Airport so departing travellers can get coffee right beside their gates. Which utility does this create most directly?
options: Possession utility
Place utility
Time utility
Form utility
questions.explanation: Place utility means having the offering available where consumers need it - here, right at the gates. Time utility would be about when it is available (for example, opening early for 5 a.m. flights).

questions.stem: Northgate Pharmacy stays open 24 hours a day so customers can fill urgent prescriptions at 3 a.m. Which utility does this primarily provide?
options: Possession utility
Place utility
Time utility
Form utility
questions.explanation: Being available WHEN consumers need the product is time utility. Place utility is about WHERE it is available, which the 24-hour schedule does not change.

questions.stem: Harmon Furniture in Winnipeg lets shoppers take a $3,000 sofa home today with 24 months of interest-free financing. Which utility does the financing offer create?
options: Possession utility
Time utility
Place utility
Form utility
questions.explanation: Possession utility is getting the product to consumers so they can own and use it, and offering credit or financing is the textbook example. Place utility concerns where the sofa is available, which the financing does not change.

questions.stem: Which type of utility does marketing NOT create directly, but only influences?
options: Place utility
Form utility
Possession utility
Time utility
questions.explanation: Form utility comes from producing the good or service, so production creates it; marketing influences it by identifying what consumers want. Marketing directly creates place, time and possession utility.

questions.stem: Golden Wheat Bakery turns flour, eggs and butter into fresh croissants every morning. Which utility does this create, and what is marketing's role in it?
options: Possession utility; marketing creates it directly by offering customers credit
Place utility; marketing creates it directly by choosing store locations
Form utility; marketing creates it directly through its promotion
Form utility; marketing influences it through insight into what consumers want
questions.explanation: Turning raw materials into a product is form utility, created by production. Marketing's role is to influence form utility by feeding consumer insights into product design, not to create it directly; promotion does not make the croissant.

questions.stem: How an individual organization directs its marketing activities and allocates its resources to benefit its customers is called:
options: micromarketing
market orientation
a value proposition
macromarketing
questions.explanation: This is micromarketing: the marketing of one organization. Macromarketing looks at the aggregate flow of a whole nation's goods and services to benefit society.

questions.stem: A University of Alberta economist studies how efficiently Canada's entire food system moves products from farms to consumers in every province, and whether that system benefits society. This is a study of:
options: micromarketing
macromarketing
relationship marketing
market orientation
questions.explanation: Examining the aggregate flow of a nation's goods to benefit society is macromarketing. Micromarketing would focus on how a single organization directs its own marketing activities.

questions.stem: Loblaw, one of Canada's largest retailers, decides how to divide its national advertising budget among its store banners. Which term best applies?
options: Neither, because budget decisions are financial rather than marketing activities
Macromarketing, because the company is very large and advertises nationally
Macromarketing, because the decision affects consumers across the whole nation
Micromarketing, because it is one organization allocating its marketing resources
questions.explanation: Micromarketing is about how an individual organization directs its marketing and allocates its resources, regardless of company size. Macromarketing is the aggregate flow of a nation's goods and services, not one large firm's national campaign.

questions.stem: Which statement about macromarketing is NOT correct?
options: It focuses on benefits to society as a whole
It concerns the aggregate flow of a nation's goods and services
It refers to marketing done by very large companies with national budgets
It looks at the overall system rather than a single organization
questions.explanation: Macromarketing is about the aggregate flow of a nation's goods and services to benefit society - a system-level view. Company size has nothing to do with it; even a giant firm's own plans are micromarketing.

questions.stem: The aggregate flow of a nation's goods and services to benefit society is called _____.
options: the societal marketing concept
macromarketing
corporate social responsibility
micromarketing
questions.explanation: Macromarketing is the society-wide, aggregate flow of a nation's goods and services. The societal marketing concept and CSR also mention society, but they describe how an individual organization should behave, not the national flow of goods.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven new and evolving marketing practices identified in Chapter 1?
options: Production orientation
Partnership marketing
Metrics and analytics
Augmented reality
questions.explanation: The seven practices are digital marketing (content, mobile, social media), augmented reality, experiential marketing, influencer marketing, partnership marketing, metrics and analytics, and new regulations and ethical considerations. Production orientation is the earliest business philosophy, not a new practice.

questions.stem: A Montreal furniture retailer's app lets shoppers point their phone at an empty corner of the living room and see a life-sized 3D sofa placed there. Which evolving practice is this?
options: Partnership marketing
Influencer marketing
Experiential marketing
Augmented reality
questions.explanation: Overlaying digital images onto the real-world view through a phone is augmented reality. Experiential marketing involves hands-on, real-world brand experiences such as events or pop-ups.

questions.stem: Glacier Water pays a Calgary fitness creator with 400,000 TikTok followers to post videos featuring its bottles in her daily workout routine. Which evolving practice is this?
options: Metrics and analytics
Experiential marketing
Influencer marketing
Partnership marketing
questions.explanation: Paying a personality with a large, trusting following to promote a brand is influencer marketing. Partnership marketing is a formal association between two brands, not a paid endorsement by an individual creator.

questions.stem: A Canadian coffee chain and a national bookseller form a formal association: co-branded cafés inside the bookstores and a shared loyalty reward. Which evolving practice is this?
options: Partnership marketing
Influencer marketing
Experiential marketing
Augmented reality
questions.explanation: Partnership marketing is the creation of formal associations between brands that contribute to each other's success, such as co-branded locations and shared rewards. Influencer marketing would rely on an individual personality's endorsement.

questions.stem: A student lists the seven new and evolving practices as: content marketing, mobile marketing, social media marketing, augmented reality, experiential marketing, influencer marketing and partnership marketing. What is wrong with this list?
options: Partnership marketing belongs to the relationship era of business philosophy, not to evolving practices
Content, mobile and social media belong under digital marketing, and metrics/analytics and regulations/ethics are missing
Influencer marketing and partnership marketing are really the same practice and should be combined
Augmented reality is just a form of experiential marketing and should not be listed as a separate item
questions.explanation: The chapter groups content, mobile and social media marketing as parts of item 1, digital marketing. The full list of seven also includes metrics and analytics and new marketing regulations and ethical considerations, which the student left out.

questions.stem: Brightwater Cosmetics runs ads on three platforms but cannot tell which one actually drives sales. Which evolving marketing practice would most directly solve this problem?
options: Experiential marketing
Augmented reality
Metrics and analytics
Partnership marketing
questions.explanation: Metrics and analytics measure marketing results, letting Brightwater compare which platform drives sales. The other practices are ways of reaching or engaging customers, not ways of measuring performance.

questions.stem: The moral principles and values that govern the actions and decisions of an individual or group are called:
options: the societal marketing concept
corporate social responsibility
laws
ethics
questions.explanation: That is the definition of ethics. Laws are rules enforced by government; CSR is the idea that organizations are accountable to society, which is broader than the moral principles guiding individual decisions.

questions.stem: Leaders at a Calgary marketing agency refuse a client's request to bury automatic-renewal fees in tiny print, saying it conflicts with the CMA Code even though no specific law clearly forbids it. Their decision is driven mainly by:
options: a regulatory force
macromarketing
customer experience management
ethical principles
questions.explanation: The agency is acting on moral principles and a code of ethics, not on a legal requirement, so ethics is the driver. A regulatory force would be a law or government rule, and the stem says no law clearly forbids the practice.

questions.stem: Which statement about codes of ethics in marketing is NOT accurate, according to the chapter?
options: Only government agencies issue codes of ethics for marketers
The CMA publishes a Canadian Marketing Code of Ethics and Standards
Many industries and professional associations have codes of ethics
Many companies have their own guidelines and codes of ethics
questions.explanation: The slides note that many companies, industries and professional associations have guidelines and codes of ethics, including the CMA's Canadian Marketing Code of Ethics and Standards. Codes are not limited to government agencies.

questions.stem: A Winnipeg supplement company's new ad is technically legal, but it implies results that the company's own studies do not support. Which statement best applies?
options: The ad is a CSR initiative, because any form of advertising has some effect on society
The ad may be legal yet unethical; codes of ethics like the CMA Code guide conduct beyond the law
The ad is a regulatory environmental force, which the company itself cannot control
Because the ad is legal, it is automatically ethical, so no code of ethics applies
questions.explanation: Laws set the legal minimum, while ethics are the moral principles governing what an individual or group believes is right, so an ad can satisfy the law and still mislead. That gap is why companies, industries and associations such as the CMA publish codes of ethics. The firm's own ad is a controllable decision, not an environmental force.

questions.stem: The Canadian Marketing Code of Ethics and Standards is published by the Chartered Institute of Marketing.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Corrected: the Canadian Marketing Code of Ethics and Standards is published by the Canadian Marketing Association (CMA). The Chartered Institute of Marketing is the UK body whose definition of marketing appears on the slides.

questions.stem: What kinds of organizations engage in marketing?
options: only those that can afford national advertising
very large and established nonprofit organizations
exclusively Fortune 1000 companies
every organization markets
virtually no organizations
questions.explanation: Every organization markets, because each needs people to engage in exchanges with it or to think or behave in a certain way - including non-profits like the Canadian Red Cross and government agencies like the Ministry of Transportation. Marketing is not limited to big advertisers or large companies.

questions.stem: Alberta's transportation ministry runs radio and billboard ads urging drivers to put their phones away while driving. Nothing is sold. Which statement best describes this campaign?
options: It is macromarketing, because a government is doing it
It is not marketing, because no product or money is exchanged
It is marketing an idea, showing that government agencies market too
It is not marketing, because only for-profit firms can market
questions.explanation: Ideas can be marketed, and governments market when they try to get people to think or behave in a certain way, like the chapter's Ministry of Transportation example. A government running a campaign is still one organization's marketing, not macromarketing (the aggregate flow of a nation's goods and services).

questions.stem: Which statement about who markets is NOT correct?
options: Non-profits such as the Canadian Red Cross engage in marketing
Services, such as dental care, can be marketed
Marketing applies only to physical goods sold for profit
Ideas, such as road safety, can be marketed
questions.explanation: Everyone markets: goods, services and ideas, for-profit and non-profit. Limiting marketing to physical goods sold for profit contradicts the chapter's 'Who markets? Everyone' slide.

questions.stem: According to Chapter 1, why is understanding marketing valuable even for students who will never work in a marketing department?
options: Because marketing affects everyone, knowing it makes us better customers, citizens and career planners
Marketing is mainly common sense, so a marketing course offers an easy and useful credit
Marketing affects only consumer-goods firms, which employ most business graduates in Canada
Marketing knowledge is legally required to obtain every Canadian business licence
questions.explanation: The career slide states that marketing affects all individuals, organizations, industries and countries, and that knowing it makes us better customers, more informed citizens and better career planners. 'Common sense' is the misconception the chapter rejects.

questions.stem: A Calgary food bank seeking donors, a city councillor seeking re-election and the Town of Banff promoting winter tourism all run campaigns. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Only Banff is marketing, because tourism is a service that visitors pay money for
All three are marketing, since organizations, individuals and places can all be marketed
Only the food bank is marketing, because charities are the only non-business exception
None of them is marketing, because none of them sells a physical product for profit
questions.explanation: Everyone markets: non-profits, individuals and places as well as firms, and the offering can be a good, service, idea, person or place. Requiring a physical product or a profit motive reflects the narrow view of marketing the chapter corrects.
